promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Latitude, longitude and the celestial sphere
The Earth's atmosphere and its effect on observation

questions.q: Starting from the surface and moving inwards, what is the correct order of the Earth's main layers?
options: Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core
Crust, outer core, mantle, inner core
Mantle, crust, inner core, outer core
Crust, inner core, mantle, outer core
questions.explain: The Earth is layered as crust, then mantle, then the liquid outer core, and finally the solid inner core.

questions.q: Which layer of the Earth is liquid?
questions.explain: The outer core is molten (liquid), whereas the inner core is solid.

questions.q: Why does the Earth have a magnetic field?
options: Movement of the liquid metal in the outer core
The solid rock of the crust is magnetic
The mantle contains large deposits of magnetite
Static charge builds up in the atmosphere
questions.explain: Convection currents in the electrically conducting liquid iron of the outer core generate the Earth's magnetic field.

questions.q: The Earth's core is composed mainly of which two metals?
questions.explain: Both the inner and outer core are made chiefly of iron and nickel.

questions.q: The inner core is hotter than the outer core, yet it is solid. Why?
options: The enormous pressure at the centre keeps it solid
It is made of a different, higher-melting metal
It has cooled down over billions of years
It is constantly cooled by the mantle above
questions.explain: The extremely high pressure at the Earth's centre raises the melting point so the inner core remains solid despite its temperature.

questions.q: What is the approximate radius of the Earth?
questions.explain: The Earth's mean radius is roughly 6400 km (about 6371 km).

questions.q: Which line on the Earth is defined as 0° latitude?
questions.explain: The equator is the line of zero latitude, midway between the poles.

questions.q: The line of 0° longitude passes through Greenwich and is called the:
questions.explain: The prime meridian, running through Greenwich, is defined as 0° longitude.

questions.q: Latitude on the Earth's surface can take values in which range?
questions.explain: Latitude is measured from 0° at the equator to 90° at each pole, north or south.

questions.q: On the celestial sphere, which coordinate is the equivalent of latitude?
questions.explain: Declination measures angle north or south of the celestial equator, just as latitude does on Earth.

questions.q: On the celestial sphere, which coordinate is the equivalent of longitude?
questions.explain: Right ascension is the celestial equivalent of longitude, measured around the celestial equator.

questions.q: What does the term 'zenith' refer to for an observer?
options: The point on the celestial sphere directly overhead
The point where the Sun rises
The northernmost point of the horizon
The centre of the celestial sphere
questions.explain: The zenith is the point on the celestial sphere directly above the observer.

questions.q: What is the ecliptic?
options: The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere over a year
The line marking the celestial equator
The circle traced by the celestial poles
The boundary between day and night on Earth
questions.explain: The ecliptic is the Sun's apparent yearly path against the background stars, reflecting the plane of Earth's orbit.

questions.q: An observer measures the altitude of Polaris (near the north celestial pole) to be 52°. What is their approximate latitude?
questions.explain: The altitude of the north celestial pole equals the observer's latitude, so 52° altitude means 52° N.

questions.q: An observer stands at latitude 30° N. At what altitude will they see the north celestial pole?
questions.explain: The altitude of the north celestial pole above the horizon equals the observer's latitude.

questions.q: Two places lie on the same latitude but differ in longitude by 30°. What is the difference in their local solar time?
questions.explain: The Earth turns 15° per hour, so 30° of longitude corresponds to a 2 hour time difference.

questions.q: Why does the daytime sky appear blue?
options: Blue light is scattered more strongly by air molecules than red light
The atmosphere emits blue light of its own
Oxygen molecules are naturally blue in colour
Blue light travels faster through the atmosphere
questions.explain: Shorter blue wavelengths are scattered much more by atmospheric molecules, so scattered blue light reaches us from all directions.

questions.q: Why do stars appear to twinkle when viewed from the ground?
options: Turbulence and movement in the atmosphere refract their light
The stars physically pulse in brightness
The Earth's rotation makes them flicker
Dust in space blocks their light intermittently
questions.explain: Moving pockets of air of differing density refract starlight in changing directions, causing the twinkling (scintillation).

questions.q: Which type of harmful radiation from the Sun is largely absorbed by ozone in the atmosphere?
questions.explain: The ozone layer absorbs much of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation before it reaches the surface.

questions.q: An astronomer wishes to observe X-rays and much of the ultraviolet light from a star. Why must this be done with a telescope in space?
options: The atmosphere absorbs these wavelengths before they reach the ground
These wavelengths are too faint to detect on Earth
Ground telescopes cannot be pointed accurately enough
Light pollution only affects these wavelengths
questions.explain: The atmosphere absorbs X-rays and most ultraviolet, so such observations require a telescope above the atmosphere.
